title: Two wings (II.4)
hook: simplicity and purity lift a person up
tomorrow: if God comes first, where does that leave your best friend?

segments.voice: Yesterday: keep yourself in peace first, then bring it to others, even the hard ones, the way one calm voice can steady a loud room. The line was peace first.

Here's a strange choice, quiet and almost odd. When the Imitation wants to say what lifts a person toward God, it doesn't reach for the famous trio, faith, hope and love. It picks two plain words: simplicity and purity. By two wings, chapter four of book two says, a person is lifted up from earthly things. Why those two, of all the virtues? And why does the book give each wing a different job, as if one alone couldn't fly?
screen: `NOT FAITH, HOPE AND LOVE?` → `SIMPLICITY AND PURITY.` → `WHY A DIFFERENT JOB FOR EACH?`

segments.voice: The answer is in the split. Simplicity belongs in the intention, the book says; purity in the affection. Simplicity is about what you aim at. Purity is about what you love. Simplicity reaches toward God; purity takes hold of him and tastes him. One wing points, the other holds, and neither flies alone. Then the payoff. If you want nothing but God's will and your neighbor's good, the chapter says, you'll be free inside, and no good action will get in your way. And here's the line that stays: if your heart were right, every creature would be a mirror of life and a book of holy teaching. Nothing is so small, it says, that it doesn't show something of God's goodness. A leaf, a dog, a cup of coffee: each one a page, if the reader's eyes are clean. As a person is inside, so they judge outside. A sour mood finds the world sour; a clean heart finds pages everywhere. Then the forge. Iron put into the fire loses its rust and glows all through; so a person who turns wholly to God loses their sluggishness and becomes new. So the puzzle solves itself. Faith, hope and love name what to have. These two name how to carry it: one plain aim, one clean love, and the rest is lift.
screen: `ONE WING POINTS, ONE HOLDS.` · `FREE INSIDE.` · `EVERY CREATURE A MIRROR.` · `IRON IN THE FIRE.` · then, large: `BY TWO WINGS A PERSON IS LIFTED UP.`

segments.voice: Pick up one ordinary thing within reach, a cup, a pen, a leaf from outside, and look at it plainly, the way the chapter says a clear heart would: as a small page about God's goodness. Don't analyze it or judge it; just look, and keep looking. If you pray, let the looking become a short thanks.
Two wings. Simplicity in what you aim at, purity in what you love: the Imitation's pair that lifts a person toward God.
Your line: two wings, one plain aim and one clean love, flying together and never alone. Sleep well.

notes: Imitation II.4 paraphrased throughout: by two wings a man is lifted from earthly things, simplicity and purity; simplicity in the intention, purity in the affection; simplicity tends to God, purity apprehends and tastes him; if you seek only God's will and your neighbor's profit you enjoy inner liberty; if your heart were right every creature would be a mirror of life and a book of holy doctrine; no creature so little and vile that it doesn't show God's goodness; as a man is inwardly, so he judges outwardly; iron in the fire loses its rust and becomes glowing, so the man who turns wholly to God puts off sluggishness and is changed into a new man. Confirm each against the Latin.
games.original gives the nominative forms 'simplicitas et puritas'; the Latin text has 'simplicitate scilicet et puritate'. Confirm the forms and the pronunciation (ecclesiastical).

v3 puzzle shape: the odd detail is that the chapter names simplicity and purity, not faith, hope and love (the theological virtues, CCC 1812–1813), and gives each a different job. 'Faith, hope and love name what to have; these two name how' is the lesson's interpretive line; a Keeper may soften it.
